bison.origin: Bison down is the winter undercoat of the American bison (Bison bison), in commerce mainly plains bison (B. b. bison) from privately managed ranch herds in the United States and Canada. Fiber is gathered as shed fiber in spring, when some ranches allow collectors to pick it, or recovered by other producer-specific methods that buyers should ask about. Hedrick (2009) estimated about 500,000 plains bison in North America, of which only about 4 percent (roughly 20,000) were in conservation herds, so nearly all commercial fiber comes from private herds. Supply is small and tied to individual producers.
bison.structure: The bison coat has two fractions: coarse outer guard hair and a dense, fine undercoat. Reported down diameters vary by source and animal, with fiber businesses citing means from roughly 15 to 22 microns and one account an average near 18.5 microns, which overlaps the range of commercial cashmere. Staple length is short, commonly cited at about 1.5 inches (about 4 cm). Like other mammalian hair it is alpha-keratin, with a cuticle of overlapping scales and a cortex of keratin intermediate filaments embedded in a sulfur-rich protein matrix. In fine undercoat fibers the medulla is typically reduced or absent, while guard hairs are thicker and usually medullated.
bison.process: Raw bison fiber arrives mixed with guard hair, dander, dust and plant matter. Processing follows the specialty-fiber route: hand sorting, gentle scouring with mild detergents, and mechanical dehairing, in which repeated carding-type actions exploit differences in length, diameter and stiffness so that guard hairs drop out. The short, slippery down is then carded and usually spun woollen-style, often blended with longer fibers such as merino, silk or cotton to aid drafting and stretch a scarce input. A US patent (No. 6,330,786) on buffalo hair yarn and fabric describes blending bison fiber with compatible fibers to extend quantity and add properties.
bison.performance: Dehaired bison down gives substantial warmth for its weight because fine, crimped fibers hold still air, and it handles moisture like other keratin fibers, absorbing water vapor while still feeling dry. Fibers below about 20 microns are generally too fine to trigger the prickle response. Its short staple is the main weakness: yarns can shed and pill unless well twisted or blended, and abrasion resistance depends on the blend partner. It chars rather than melts. It accepts acid and other protein dye classes, although the natural brown is often left undyed. It shares protein-fiber vulnerabilities to moth larvae, alkaline detergents, chlorine bleach and felting under heat and agitation.
bison.identify: Burn behavior (indicative only; test small samples with care) is that of hair: slow burning, a burnt-hair odor and brittle ash. Under the microscope bison down appears as fine, pigmented keratin fibers, and any residual guard hairs are far thicker and medullated. Microscopy alone may not separate bison down from yak or other bovid down reliably, so origin claims in high-value goods should rest on DNA-based species testing, which is used for luxury animal fibers, together with documentation from the ranch or processor.
bison.labeling: Bison is not among the specialty fibers named in the Wool Products Labeling Act, so bison content is disclosed under the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act rules. Under 16 CFR 303.6, the name of a fur-bearing animal may be used with the word fiber, hair or blend when that fiber is 5 percent or more of the product, and hair of animals other than those the rule lists may be described collectively as fur fiber when no representation is made about the animal. In the EU, Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 places such hair in the animal or horsehair category, where the animal may be named.
bison.past: North American bison numbered in the many millions in the mid-nineteenth century and were reduced to near extinction by the middle 1880s. Hedrick (2009) notes that plains bison survived mainly through five private ranch herds and a small herd in what is now Yellowstone National Park, so today's plains bison descend from fewer than 100 founders, and many herds carry cattle ancestry from crossbreeding promoted in the late 1800s and early 1900s. Conservation genetics continues: a 2022 mtDNA survey of 14 US and Canadian herds and a 2026 genome-wide study of herds reintroduced at American Prairie from 2005 onward. The down-yarn niche is recent and depends on this ranching base.
